noticias.titulo: US hotline to report cartel activities slammed as foreign interference by Mexico
noticias.resumen: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum denounced on Friday the US hotline for reporting drug cartel activities as foreign interference.
noticias.texto:
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum denounced on Friday the US hotline for reporting drug cartel activities as foreign interference.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum lodged a formal complaint with the US for setting up a hotline dedicated to reporting drug cartel activities and corrupt officials in Mexico.
The US Drug Enforcement Administration said on Wednesday it would open channels for Mexican citizens to anonymously report individuals, public officials and money laundering networks linked to the Sinaloa cartel. The US has previously designated the Mexican cartel as a terrorist organisation.
The announcement stirred the ongoing struggle between the US and Mexico over who has the right to take action against cartels in Mexico.
"We have made it very clear that our relationship with the United States is one of coordination, not subordination," Sheinbaum said.
Sheinbaum said it had lodged a formal complaint with US Ambassador Ron Johnson, as she slams the hotline as a form of interference.
"We have to say what we are thinking, and furthermore it is an obligation to do so because we have to defend our sovereignty," she said in a news conference.
'We're all fed up'
Juan Manuel Partida Valdez, president of the Sinaloa Journalists Association, has welcomed this US hotline by being among the first to write to the tip line on Thursday.
He said he sent information about alleged ties between politicians from the Sinaloa region and criminal groups. Partida Valdez said that he got a quick response and that his move was motivated by the authorities' failure to put an end to violence and corruption in northern Mexican regions.
"I talk to so many people — in the streets, on social media, on WhatsApp and in chats — and you realise what people think: We’re all fed up," the 67-year-old journalist said on Friday. "We’re fed up with narco-governments."
In May, Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya — a powerful figure of Sheinbaum's party — was forced to step down after he was indicted by the US on drug-trafficking charges. He returned to office in August to step down another time just a day after coming back.
For Partida Valdez, this case is one of the main reasons that led him to reach out to the tip line, saying it was a "very clear example of what we’re suffering because of these governments that do absolutely nothing but protect criminals."
"This whole song and dance about sovereignty is just collusion with the politicians tied to drug trafficking who are being protected in our country," he added.
While several warned of the dangers of the US DEA's strategy, some academics and politicians like Lilly Téllez, a senator for Mexico’s National Action Party, a weakened opposition party, have celebrated the line.
The politician from the US-Mexico border state of Sonora said on X that it was "a good way to cooperate against the common enemy of both countries" and strengthens efforts to combat cartels.
A balancing act for Sheinbaum
Despite the significant expansion of security cooperation between the two countries, US President Donald Trump's administration has continued putting intense pressure on Sheinbaum to crack down on her country's drug gangs.
Trump has repeatedly threatened to take unilateral action against Mexican cartels if Mexico didn't step up against organised crime.
A difficult position for Sheinbaum, as she wishes to extend a free-trade deal with the US and Canada, while staying firm on her country's sovereignty and security.
Last week, Mexico's military captured a drug lord named Fausto Isidro Meza alias Chapo Isidro, one of the FBI's most-wanted fugitives.
Sheinbaum's left-wing government has insisted on keeping the drug lord at home to judge him before considering a US extradition.
Homicide rates have plunged in Mexico as the government took out several top cartel bosses, often using US intelligence to do so.

noticias.titulo: France to create strategic rare earth reserves, with resilience coming at a cost
noticias.resumen: France aims to build reserves of critical minerals and urges Europe to invest more. Researcher Frédéric Jeannin says these stocks should protect France from market shocks and prepare its industry for a possible armed conflict.
noticias.texto:
France aims to build reserves of critical minerals and urges Europe to invest more. Researcher Frédéric Jeannin says these stocks should protect France from market shocks and prepare its industry for a possible armed conflict.
A late-term announcement, at a time when France and Europe are facing tensions that are disrupting global trade and supply chains. Emmanuel Macron is launching the creation of reserves of rare earths and critical metals to reduce the country's dependence and anticipate shortages. Three key sectors are targeted: defence, the automotive industry and aerospace.
The plan, seen by Euronews, was unveiled at the start of the week during a meeting at the Élysée called "Protect France", which brought together around 15 industry bosses.
Implementation of this mechanism of strategic reserves and "joint purchases" has been entrusted to the Caisse des dépôts, the state's financial arm.
Companies will be required to play their part by diversifying their supply sources, or risk seeing their public support cut. Mechanisms for "price guarantees" will also be offered "to give producers visibility".
But many questions remain open. At this stage, the challenge is to define precisely the storage scenarios, the stakeholders involved and the minerals for which needs are most urgent.
Frédéric Jeannin, a researcher at the IRIS think tank and co-head of the Energy and Raw Materials programme, stresses the importance of this preparatory work: "The state needs to draw up a list of what is strategic, which companies it wants to supply," he told Euronews in an interview.
Physical reserves or virtual ones based on purchase commitments? In the expert's view, "we can have both". The point of this "insurance", he explains, is to allow the country to cope with two types of threat: "a security shock or a market shock".
"We wonder whether China has a better picture of our industry than we do"
According to Frédéric Jeannin, these reserves must first serve to "strengthen our resilience" to international raw materials markets, where access to resources is "less and less certain, at least at an economically acceptable price".
China currently dominates the sector, notably thanks to its vast refining capacity, the energy geopolitics researcher points out.
While the Élysée describes dependence on supplies as a possible "tool of coercion and threat", Frédéric Jeannin sees these reserves as a "safety buffer". They would make it possible to cushion price swings that could be triggered by decisions taken in Beijing.
China has a legal arsenal that allows it to block the export of its critical raw materials depending on their end use and final recipient, whenever Beijing considers that these exports run counter to its interests.
Export licences thus enable it to screen sales on a case by case basis, without having to impose a blanket embargo that would hurt its own mining companies.
The researcher also highlights the level of transparency demanded of buyers regarding the processing and value chain of materials imported from China, "to the point of demanding information that amounts to industrial secrets".
"We wonder whether China has a better picture of our industry than we do", observes Frédéric Jeannin.
Reserves to hold out in the event of war
Frédéric Jeannin identifies a second factor: the prospect of an open conflict with Russia.
The aim is first of all very concrete: "We need to guarantee that raw materials will be available on our soil, ideally through physical stockpiles, to supply the defence industry".
"But there is also a psychological dimension", he adds: it is a way of telling a potential "hostile actor" that France is able to withstand a crisis, "with stocks available, with components available, with raw materials available that would allow us to hold out for a certain period".
How long that period would be remains to be seen. Although the scheme is designed to be long term, the Élysée says it has already "generated" nearly 7 billion euros of investment in France.
Even though French and American industry are not comparable in size, the United States provides a benchmark. Last February, Washington announced the creation of its strategic reserve, "Project Vault" ("projet coffre-fort"), worth 12 billion dollars. It is intended to cover the equivalent of two months of national consumption.
"Seven billion is a good start. We are talking about amounts that will run into billions of euros", notes Frédéric Jeannin. But, he emphasises, it is still necessary to know who these investments will benefit and according to which criteria.
"What companies need to keep in mind, and indeed, I would say, what citizens need to keep in mind, is that this resilience is necessary today and that it has a cost", the expert stresses.
"Our industries have to factor in a cost of resilience to make sure we have what we need on our territory. It will be more expensive, but it is necessary to protect us in the event of a crisis", he concludes.
"Europe is making a strategic mistake"
Warnings about the need to build up strategic reserves are not new, including at European level.
The European Union has identified 34 critical raw materials, 17 of them considered "strategic", for which demand is expected to outstrip supply in the years ahead.
For these strategic materials, dependence on third countries is high. China supplies the EU with 85% of its samarium, which when combined with cobalt forms magnets that are vital for electric motors; Turkey provides 99% of its boron, used in particular in ballistic protection; and South Africa delivers 41% of its manganese, essential for steel production, according to a map (source in French) from the European Commission.
In early November, Members of the European Parliament backed (source in French) the creation of a Competitiveness Fund, currently under negotiation as part of the EU budget for 2028 to 2034. France wants to earmark 25 billion euros out of the roughly 300 billion euro envelope, in order to stabilise prices and build up European reserves.
But asserting Paris's priorities within the European budget is proving difficult. Thursday's extraordinary European summit even descended into a full-blown drama, laying bare divisions among the 27 member states. The flashpoint was a proposal by the President of the European Council, Antonio Costa, to cut around 200 billion euros from the initial budget draft put forward by the Commission.
Emmanuel Macron denounced a "strategic mistake" in response to the cuts, which were supported notably by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
"We are about to formalise a gap in European public investment compared with China and the United States", the French president said at a press conference in Brussels.
"When it comes to having a budget that matches our ambitions, there is no one to follow us", he lamented.
Emmanuel Macron threatened to pull out of the budget negotiations if no agreement emerges by the end of the year. He refuses to let the talks drag on and encroach on the French presidential election, whose first round is scheduled for 18 April 2027.
The fate of France's strategic reserves will also depend on who succeeds him at the Élysée.
Nathan Joubioux contributed to this article.

noticias.titulo: Russia says it downed hundreds of drones as Ukraine reports first laser interception of a jet drone
noticias.resumen: Ukraine says a privately developed laser shot down a Russian jet-powered drone for the first time. Meanwhile, Russian strikes continued overnight into Saturday, damaging transport infrastructure in Dnipro and injuring five people across the Dnipropetrovsk region, regional officials say.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine says a privately developed laser shot down a Russian jet-powered drone for the first time. Meanwhile, Russian strikes continued overnight into Saturday, damaging transport infrastructure in Dnipro and injuring five people across the Dnipropetrovsk region, regional officials say.
Russian air defences shot down hundreds of Ukrainian drones heading towards the Moscow region overnight, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Saturday.
The Moscow mayor said more than 460 drones headed towards the region between late Friday and early Saturday.
His statement came after Ukraine’s state-backed defence group Brave1 said on Friday that Ukraine had used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered drone "for the first time".
Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov published footage earlier this week showing a target crashing in a fireball. He said the Blysk laser system, developed by Carmine Sky, had been protecting a critical infrastructure facility when it shot down a Russian Geran jet drone.
Ukraine and Russia have intensified their drone and missile attacks in recent months as the war continues into its fifth year and the United States seeks talks to end the fighting.
Previously, Ukrainian air defence teams have used machine guns and shoulder-fired missiles to bring down Russian drones.
Brave1 said a private air defence team operated the laser and cautioned that “a first successful interception does not mean the technology is ready for mass deployment”.
Russian strikes continued overnight into Saturday, with more than 20 drone attacks across four districts of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the oblast's military administration, said on Telegram.
The attacks damaged transport infrastructure in the city of Dnipro and injured five people across the region, including a 15-year-old boy.
Earlier this week, Russian forces struck residential buildings and an educational institution in Kharkiv, in the country's northeast, killing at least three people in a wider ballistic missile and drone assault that also caused casualties in Kyiv and other regions.

noticias.titulo: Ping pongonomics: Can table-tennis bring strangers together to talk about the art of play?
noticias.resumen: A new exhibition at London's Saatchi Gallery is inviting visitors to put down their phones and talk with strangers over ping pong. Created by British-French artist Charlotte Colbert, 'Conversations with Strangers' features sculptural tables designed to encourage spontaneous and sporting encounters.
noticias.texto:
A new exhibition at London's Saatchi Gallery is inviting visitors to put down their phones and talk with strangers over ping pong. Created by British-French artist Charlotte Colbert, 'Conversations with Strangers' features sculptural tables designed to encourage spontaneous and sporting encounters.
What if a game of ping pong could help strangers connect? That is the idea behind a new interactive exhibition at London's Saatchi Gallery, where visitors are being encouraged to put down their phones, pick up a bat and play.
Called Conversations with Strangers, the exhibition is the work of British-French artist and filmmaker Charlotte Colbert. It features specially designed sculptural ping pong tables, transforming the traditional gallery experience into a space for play and face-to-face interaction.
The artist says the exhibition builds on her recent experience creating large-scale public sculptures in unexpected locations, including New York and Egypt.
Bringing that approach into the gallery, Colbert wanted to create an environment where visitors could interact with the artwork rather than simply observe it. "It aims to be part-gallery, part-playground and a connecter," she explains.
For Colbert, the idea carries a wider message about human relationships in the digital age. "In the age of algorithms what information we get and who we speak to is so controlled that chatting to strangers is a form of defiance. A glitch in the matrix that opens up a whole world of possibility," she says.
And she sees table tennis as a particularly effective way of encouraging people to reconnect with the present. "Ping pong is a form of instant mindfulness. It immediately forces you in the here and now. Play is the basis of all reinvention - it frees the mind and body - even for just a second and in that space allows possibility to exist."
Timing is everything in life and the exhibition comes as table tennis is enjoying a renaissance in France due to the Olympic triumphs of the Lebrun brothers, Felix and Alexis. Actor Timothée Chalamet's starring role in Marty Supreme also put the sport in the global spotlight.
"That was a game changer for ping pong!" says Colbert. "I think even Zinedine Zidane came to watch. Epic. And off the back of Marty Supreme it's a real table tennis renaissance.
Colbert argues that play should not be seen as something reserved for children, but as an essential part of creativity and human connection.
Alongside the exhibition, Colbert has created a limited-edition collection with Art of Ping Pong, featuring playable wall-mounted tables, bats and nets decorated with her signature surrealist designs.
Conversations with Strangers runs at Saatchi Gallery until January 2027. Admission is free.

noticias.titulo: How sifting through sewage could help scientists spot the next pandemic
noticias.resumen: Swiss scientists already use wastewater testing to detect flu, COVID-19 and RSV. Next, they want to use it to flag unknown threats.
noticias.texto:
Swiss scientists already use wastewater testing to detect flu, COVID-19 and RSV. Next, they want to use it to flag unknown threats.
Swiss scientists are trying to identify pandemic health threats faster — by expanding the data they get from sifting through our sewage.
People shed traces of viruses when they use the bathroom, wash their hands, brush their teeth or take a shower. When that wastewater gets to treatment plants, scientists take small samples and test them for virus fragments.
Wastewater surveillance has long been used to detect how polioviruses, drug-resistant bacteria and illegal drugs are circulating in a community, serving as an early warning system for public health authorities.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, wastewater surveillance helped researchers identify which variants were spreading and when waves were at their peak, regardless of whether people had symptoms.
In Switzerland, researchers now routinely track coronaviruses, influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) using wastewater samples from 10 treatment plants, covering 22% of the population. That’s down from around 100 plants during the COVID-19 pandemic.
They use the data to warn hospitals about a coming uptick in illnesses, so they can decide about staffing, masking and other measures. By sequencing the virus fragments, researchers can also anticipate how severe Switzerland's flu season may be and identify how effective vaccines and monoclonal antibodies — which are used to prevent and treat certain infections, like RSV — are against a particular viral strain.
“Sequences can tell us, are monoclonals or vaccines working well, or do we anticipate there's a problem, so we should change that in some way?” Tanja Stadler, who heads the Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (ETH Zürich), told Euronews.
“If we see such mutations, we can highlight that,” added Stadler, who also leads public health work for a scientific advisory group to the Swiss government.
Now, her team believes wastewater surveillance could help identify the next pandemic-level threat.
They are developing tools to detect all circulating viruses — not just a select few. If all goes well, they’ll even be able to detect Disease X, the placeholder name for an unknown pathogen with pandemic potential.
“Right now, we are going very specific to the pathogens at hand,” Stadler said. “We pretty much filter out everything SARS-CoV-2 (the virus that causes COVID-19), measure how often it is there and how it looks.”
With the broader approach, they would filter out and sequence every virus detected in wastewater, including unknown strains. “If there's then some pathogen X, a new pandemic strain, we would capture it as much as influenza or SARS-CoV-2,” she said.
Stadler also wants to get information from wastewater samples about who actually shed the virus fragments they detect. If a bird sheds avian influenza, for example, it’s much less worrisome than if the virus fragment sticks to human cells, indicating the source was a human.
Bird flu has jumped from animals to people in recent years in Europe and North America, but there is no evidence of sustained person-to-person transmission. If the virus mutates to a point where it can easily spread between people, that would be a major global health threat.
“That’s a huge pandemic risk,” Stadler said.
Eventually, she said wastewater data could also give scientists clues about how well-protected the community is against a particular virus, by measuring the antibodies in sewage samples.
These developments could arrive within the next two to six years, Stadler said, but only if funding remains stable.
The group’s work is already in high demand. They publish a near-real time wastewater surveillance dashboard for hospitals, public health agencies and pharmaceutical companies — and if it goes down, they hear about it quickly.
“Occasionally, for whatever reasons, it may be down a couple hours, and we have both clinicians [and] industry then directly emailing: ‘What's wrong?’” Stadler said. It’s “a good thing that we know it's being used.”

noticias.titulo: What now for the EU budget after a chaotic, inconclusive summit?
noticias.resumen: A chaotic summit in Brussels has raised serious doubt over whether EU leaders will abandon their red lines and agree on a new budget by the end of the year. Here's what to expect.
noticias.texto:
A chaotic summit in Brussels has raised serious doubt over whether EU leaders will abandon their red lines and agree on a new budget by the end of the year. Here's what to expect.
This week's special summit in Brussels was never meant to produce a final deal on the European Union's next seven-year budget.
Instead, its aim was to encourage leaders to move beyond their entrenched positions and much-repeated red lines in search of a possible compromise.
None of that happened.
Leaders holed themselves up in the trenches, pointed the finger at each other and refused to budge one single inch. It did not take long for the meeting to descend into disarray, with simmering tensions bursting into the open for all to see.
Plans to continue the talks on Friday were scrapped as it became clear that the hoped-for breakthrough remained out of reach.
The chaotic, inconclusive summit offers an ominous preview of what will (or not) happen when leaders meet again on 17-18 December to attempt the final deal. Diplomats and officials in Brussels presage a "blood-on-the-walls" marathon that will likely stretch into the weekend – and perhaps into the following week.
Here's where things are now and what to expect next.
What's on the table?
The bitter fight over the next EU budget (2028-2034) began last year when the European Commission presented a nearly €2 trillion proposal with record spending on defence, border controls, green energy, innovation and foreign policy.
The Commission revamped the budget's traditional structure, which allocates cash for specific programmes over a seven-year horizon, to make it more flexible and reactive to unforeseen crises. The lessons from the pandemic, Russia's war on Ukraine and natural disasters weighed heavily on the thinking.
Although the new structure was preserved, the €2 trillion volume was successively cut by the Cypriot and Irish presidencies to make it more politically palatable.
The last cut was inflicted by European Council President António Costa, who tabled a €1.78 trillion budget in current prices – a 10% reduction of roughly €204 billion.
Costa heavily cut Heading 2 (Competitiveness) and Heading 3 (Global Europe) and largely spared Heading 1, which includes agriculture and cohesion policies.
Who's who in the fight?
The budget has split member states into two irreconcilable camps.
On the one side, the seven "frugals": Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden. All of these are net payers in the budget and are determined to slash the overall size. They also want to focus common spending on modern-day priorities, hence their euphemistic nickname: "modernisers".
For them, Costa's proposed €204 billion reduction is unacceptable. The group has now demanded an additional €50 billion decrease.
"This won't stop at €204 billion. It will be even less. How much less it will be is still open," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said at the summit.
On the other side, the 17 "Friends of Cohesion": Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia and Spain. Most of these countries are net recipients of EU funds and want to preserve ambitious expenditure for both traditional and modern policies.
For them, Costa has cut too much, and nothing less can be tolerated.
"We are fighting for a good budget for our region. We are taking action, and we are not backing down," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said, striking a combative tone.
France, a net payer that receives hefty farming subsidies, has not picked a side but is adamantly opposed to any drastic devaluation. French President Emmanuel Macron slammed Costa's €204 billion cuts as a "strategic mistake" that would make Europe more dependent on the United States and China.
A similar warning was issued by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who does not have a vote but plays a crucial technical role. "We need to stay true to the priorities we have collectively agreed on for the past years," she said.
Ireland and Luxembourg are non-committal, though they are seen as more frugal-friendly.
So what now?
The focus now turns back to Costa, whose authority and credibility as European Council president will be defined by the outcome of these negotiations.
"We need to continue to work and to try to bring all the member states closer. In any case, as you know, we need unanimity to approve the new budget," he said.
"That means that all member states need to agree with each other."
Costa and his team have drawn two conclusions: the "frugals" will request further cuts and the "cohesion friends" will oppose any reductions of H1 (agriculture and cohesion). This puts H2 (competitiveness) and H3 (global Europe), the two envelopes that the "frugals" want to boost, on the chopping block.
However, some "cohesion friends", like Poland and the Baltics, are ready to fight for H2 because it includes funding for defence and security.
Another point of contention that remains glaringly unresolved is the EU-wide taxes, also known as "new own resources", to bring additional revenue into the budget.
Costa has proposed a package of five taxes – digital services, carbon-intensive imports, electronic waste, tobacco products and the Emissions Trading System (ETS) – to collect around €60 billion per year.
So far, no tax has garnered the necessary unanimity. Ireland and Malta, for instance, are firmly opposed to the digital tax, while Poland is dead-set against the ETS.
The fact that these own resources have a distinctly uneven impact on member states also raises eyebrows.
If the taxes are pared down and fail to raise €60 billion per year, Costa will have no choice but to cut the budget even deeper to offset the loss.
How hard is the deadline?
Costa has repeatedly urged leaders to agree on the new budget by the end of the year at the very latest. This, he says, is necessary to have enough time to negotiate with the European Parliament, finalise the multiple pieces of legislation and prepare national administrations for the new structure before the budget kicks in in January 2028.
But there is an additional factor: next year will see high-stakes elections in France, Italy, Greece and Poland, among others, that could make it impossible to take key decisions.
Macron threatened to pull out of the talks altogether if leaders fail to reach a deal this year, arguing he would lack the democratic legitimacy to continue the process in early 2027.
The first round of the French presidential election is slated for 18 April. Far-right firebrand Marine Le Pen, who leads opinion polls, has vowed to slash the EU budget.
"We are not prepared to reach a deal at any cost. We can conclude by 31st December, but that is the absolute limit," Macron said at the summit.
Not everyone is convinced. Some see the December deadline as artificial and politically motivated, rather than a hardcore legal constraint. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, from the "cohesion friends", and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, from the "frugals", say what truly matters is the quality, not the timing, of the deal.
What about Ukraine?
The budget fight has overlapped with efforts to provide Ukraine with a new €45 billion support loan to plug its 2027 wartime deficit. Russia's relenteless attacks have wreaked havoc on the economy and raised costs for Kyiv's budget and army.
This week's summit was expected to address both issues, but the budget sucked the energy in the room and relegated Ukraine to the backseat.
There was one important development, though: Bulgaria confirmed it will join the new loan on condition that it is exempted from footing the military bill.
This leaves three countries – Slovakia, Hungary and the Czech Republic – as the main holdouts. The three already have an opt-out from the previous €90 billion loan.
"I expect that when we meet in December, we will sit down to discuss this," Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said at the end of the summit.
"The €45 billion ceiling for the loan will be established, and whoever wants to will sign up to it. Slovakia, however, will not participate."
In yet another layer of complication, the next budget will determine the collective payment of the accrued interest from the two loans, estimated at €6 billion per year.
Several leaders also want to open a debate on how to strengthen long-term financing for Ukraine in the next budget, be it for a longer war or a post-war recovery.
Merz insists the budget cannot be closed without settling the Ukraine question at the same time.

noticias.titulo: US military fires at a ship that violated blockade of Iranian ports
noticias.resumen: US military maintained a "strict" blockade of Iranian ports by firing at a ship that violated the naval containment on Thursday.
noticias.texto:
US military maintained a "strict" blockade of Iranian ports by firing at a ship that violated the naval containment on Thursday.
An American aircraft fired at a Palau-flagged ship violating Washington's blockade of Iranian ports on Thursday.
The US military announced on Friday it had struck the Pacific Archer in its stern with "precision munitions" while the ship was attempting to run the blockade.
"The ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled, and the civilian crew was unharmed," the US statement said.
The Pacific Archer had left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas in the Strait of Hormuz to be rapidly intercepted in the Gulf of Oman, just after the strait, according to the statement.
The US forces' Central Command said it "continues to strictly enforce the blockade," which allowed them to disable six ships and redirect 158 others.
Hormuz remains closed
This US blockade has been in action since mid-July following the collapse of a short-lived agreement with Iran.
On its side, Iran has maintained its own blockade on ships transiting through the Strait of Hormuz. In recent weeks, the country's forces have signalled multiple ships catching fire while attempting to use routes that Tehran considers off-limits.
On Monday, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei vowed to use all means at the country's disposal to counter the US blockade.
Diplomatic efforts attempting to resolve the crisis — which broke out in February with US and Israeli strikes on Iran — have remained stalled.
Iran has said that Hormuz could reopen within two days if the US agreed to its demands, which include the lifting of the blockade.

noticias.titulo: Italy is turning into a solar powerhouse. But what happens when the sun goes down?
noticias.resumen: “Italy has plenty of sun, but it still runs its evenings on expensive gas – batteries can change that.”
noticias.texto:
“Italy has plenty of sun, but it still runs its evenings on expensive gas – batteries can change that.”
Italy’s reliance on sky-high gas prices could be eased by a boom in battery storage, helping lower energy bills for cash-strapped households.
Despite achieving 49 per cent of its electricity share from renewable sources last year, the country is still dependent on gas – the most expensive way to generate electricity – when demand is at its highest.
This tends to be around 8pm when people come home from work and school, which coincides with a dip in solar generation due to a lack of sunlight.
A new analysis from energy think tank Ember, in collaboration with Cleantech for Italy and Energy Square, found pairing solar and wind power with battery storage systems (BESS) is becoming central to Italy’s power system – and the country needs to act fast.
How batteries can slash Italy’s electricity prices
The study found that even under conservative estimates, renewable power stored and shifted to the evening could cost €106/MW against €210/MWh for gas power at October 2026 gas prices.
This means that battery storage could cut electricity prices by up to 49 per cent compared to producing electricity with a typical gas power plant.
“Italy has plenty of sun, but it still runs its evenings on expensive gas,” says Beatrice Petrovich, a principal energy analyst at Ember.
“Batteries change that, carrying low-cost renewable power into the hours when prices peak. Italy is already one of the most advanced EU countries for batteries connected to the power grid."
Batteries met an average of 2.8 per cent of Italy’s peak demand in the first half of 2026, more than double the level in the first half of last year, and are already displacing soaring gas prices.
This may seem small in comparison to fossil power’s 40 per cent, but analysts say it could grow quickly as contracted projects start to come online.
This is already happening across the EU, as nations scramble to balance renewable power and reduce curtailment (when clean energy is wasted due to supply outstripping demand).
Take Bulgaria, which has grown its grid-scale battery fleet from almost nothing in 2024 to almost 3 GWh by the end of 2025 and 16 GWh by August 2026 – overtaking Italy despite having a much smaller power system.
In the first half of 2026, batteries routinely supplied over a quarter of Bulgaria’s electricity demand (28 per cent) during the 8pm evening demand peak, up from four per cent one year prior, while fossil power’s share of the evening peak fell from 35 per cent to 31 per cent.
Bulgaria experienced less extreme price spikes during the summer 2026 heatwave than neighbouring countries, with strong battery discharge being one of the main drivers.
‘Storage and new generation need to develop together’
The price of electricity remains tied to volatile fossil fuels due to what is known as the merit order principle.
This ensures that electricity prices are based on the most expensive power plant still needed to meet demand.
So, if Italy’s electricity needs cannot be covered solely by clean energy (which it can’t when there is a lack of wind and sunshine), more expensive sources like coal or gas step in.
As Michele Torsello, director of Energy Square, points out – Italy’s challenge therefore isn’t to simply install more batteries, but to build an electricity system that “makes the most” of renewable energy.
“Storage, grids and new generation need to develop together,” he adds.
“As renewables grow, the value of each investment increasingly depends on the others. Capturing these synergies is key to translating this progress into lower costs for the electricity system as a whole.”

noticias.titulo: Where are the best places in Europe to observe the winter solstice?
noticias.resumen: The winter solstice falls on the shortest day and the longest night of the year, and across Europe this is marked with celebrations steeped in tradition.
noticias.texto:
The winter solstice falls on the shortest day and the longest night of the year, and across Europe this is marked with celebrations steeped in tradition.
Europe’s winter calendar isn’t just about chilly temperatures, cream-topped cups of hot chocolate and donning gloves. Across the continent, the festive season is also a time to observe the winter solstice.
The astronomical event marking the shortest day and longest night of the year in the Northern Hemisphere derives its name from the Latin word “sōlstitium”, which means the “sun stands still”.
While the December date it’s celebrated on varies slightly from country to country in Europe, centuries-old traditions are what’s common, including bonfires and parades to ward away the gloom and doom of the year and ushering in new beginnings and light.
From England to Latvia, the occasion continues to draw visitors. Here’s where to set off to in Europe if you have your sights on celebrating the winter solstice.
Must-visit destinations for the Winter Solstice
Stone Circle at Stonehenge, England
One of Europe’s most iconic destinations to observe the winter solstice is at Stonehenge’s Stone Circle.
The mysterious monument, which has a history spanning 4,500 years from the Neolithic and Bronze Age, may have been built especially to mark the occasion with experts noting that the stones are shaped and set up to frame the midwinter sunset at the time of winter solstice.
Archaeologists also estimate that Neolithic people may have gathered at Stonehenge during the winter solstice to have feasts and take part in celebrations.
On 22 December 2026, sunrise in Stonehenge will be at 8:09 am and entry will be free for the scores of spiritualists and tourists that will gather for the year’s shortest day.
The ‘Old Solstice’ in northern Europe and Nordic countries
Observed on 13 December in countries like Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Norway, St. Lucia’s day is a Scandinavian and Nordic tradition to usher in light during the darkest days of the year.
With roots in both Christian and older Norse folkloric tradition, the occasion honours the martyrdom of St. Lucia, whose name means “light”. The date originates from medieval Scandinavia’s winter solstice according to the Julian Calendar.
In Sweden, “Luciatåg” processions are broadcast on national television as well as held across the country’s schools, churches, town halls and celebrated in homes and offices. Observes dress in white robes and a young girl portrays the Saint, wearing a crown and holding a candle.
In Helsinki, Finland, the Lucia crowning ceremony and parade attracts around 30,000 people each year. A young girl is chosen to represent Saint Lucia and given the duty of leading parades through the city.
Meanwhile in Norway, “Lucia-dagen” is marked with the tradition of eating “lussekatt” s-shaped buns, baked with saffron. Traditionally only eaten on St. Lucia’s Day, the yellow colour was once associated with light, purity and protection from evil in medieval Europe.
Koliada in Slavic countries
In countries like Czechia and Poland, you may catch parades of people dressed as goats, bulls and even evil spirits as part of Koliada, or Koleda as it’s otherwise known, celebrations.
Also having roots as a pre-Christian festival to mark the winter solstice, in ancient times, a procession of young people, called “the koledari” in Czechia, dressed in costumes that were thought to ward off demons.
They would also sing carols for each house they passed by to cleanse it, and, in turn, homeowners would give them sweets and money.
**Newgrange, Ireland **
This mysterious kidney-shaped mount in County Meath, Ireland, is thought to have once served as a religious and ceremonial hub among Neolithic people and took 300 people to build over 20 years.
One of the oldest astronomically-oriented structures in the world, a beam of light spears into the roof-box and reaches up to 19 metres along the passage and illuminates the chamber during the mornings of the winter solstice. This happens from 19-23 December each year and lasts for 17 minutes.
The ancient ceremony has a limited capacity, with a controlled lottery selecting fewer than 40 people who can come accompanied by a guest to witness the solar phenomenon.
**Yule Logs, Latvia **
Across Latvia, it’s tradition to don a mask and drag a yule log around one’s home or neighbourhood before burning it in a communal fire to mark the solstice on 21 December.
This is thought to represent shedding the hardship, adversities and misfortunes of the soon-to-be previous year and chase away evil spirits.
In the country’s capital, Rīga, at the Town Hall in the old town, this tradition unfolds with singing, dancing and traditional Latvian games as the symbolic log is rolled through several streets before being burned in a large bonfire.

noticias.titulo: Russia charges air force deputy chief with taking large bribe
noticias.resumen: Yuri Grekhov, 64, who oversaw procurement of aircraft, missiles and air defence systems and has been under EU sanctions since 2022, is a serving officer, unlike most of the more than a dozen senior defence figures detained since Andrei Belousov replaced Sergei Shoigu as defence minister in 2024.
noticias.texto:
Yuri Grekhov, 64, who oversaw procurement of aircraft, missiles and air defence systems and has been under EU sanctions since 2022, is a serving officer, unlike most of the more than a dozen senior defence figures detained since Andrei Belousov replaced Sergei Shoigu as defence minister in 2024.
Russia has arrested Aerospace Forces (VKS) Deputy Commander in Chief Yuri Grekhov on charges of accepting a particularly large bribe, the latest in a series of corruption cases against senior military figures since the country changed its defence minister in 2024.
Grekhov, 64, oversaw procurement of aircraft, munitions, missiles and air defence systems. The charge carries a prison sentence of up to 15 years under Russian law.
Grekhov has been on the EU sanctions list since 2022, when Brussels deemed him responsible for Russian strikes on military and civilian sites after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A career military officer since 1979, Grekhov became deputy commander in chief under Alexander Chaiko in 2021, after commanding the air and missile defence forces from 2018 to 2021.
Unlike most of the other officials detained in recent cases, Grekhov is a serving officer, making him one of the most senior figures to come under investigation while still in post.
The VKS controls Russia's military aviation, space operations and strategic missile defence, and has played a central role in strikes on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure throughout the war.
String of arrests since Shoigu's removal
At least a dozen senior ministry employees and generals have been detained or become criminal suspects since Andrei Belousov replaced the dismissed Sergei Shoigu as defence minister in 2024.
Belousov, an economist with no military background, was appointed with an explicit mandate to impose financial discipline on the defence ministry in what Moscow said was part of a crackdown on corruption within military ranks.
The most prominent case was the arrest of former Deputy Defence Minister Timur Ivanov in April 2024.
A close associate of Shoigu for more than a decade, Ivanov was convicted of taking a particularly large bribe in Defence Ministry contracting work, embezzlement and money laundering. He was sentenced to 13 years in a penal colony and fined 100 million roubles (€1 million).
Former first deputy defence minister Ruslan Tsalikov was detained in March 2026 on charges of creating a criminal organisation, embezzlement and laundering budget funds. In November he received 10 years in a high-security penal colony and a fine of 500 million roubles (€5 million).
Others detained for bribery and embezzlement include former Deputy Chief of the General Staff Vadim Shamarin, sentenced to seven years, former head of the Defence Ministry's Main Personnel Directorate Yuri Kuznetsov, sentenced to 12 years, and former Deputy Defence Ministers Dmitry Bulgakov and Pavel Popov.
Several Western governments have assessed that the prosecutions also serve to selectively remove officials who have fallen out of favour with the Kremlin.
The pattern of cases allows Moscow to present itself as enforcing accountability while using criminal charges as a tool of internal political control.

noticias.titulo: Best and worst places in Europe for young people to find a job
noticias.resumen: Unemployment among 15- to 24-year-olds in the EU is three times the rate among people aged 25 to 74. Where in Europe is youth unemployment highest, and what helps explain the gap between the two age groups?
noticias.texto:
Unemployment among 15- to 24-year-olds in the EU is three times the rate among people aged 25 to 74. Where in Europe is youth unemployment highest, and what helps explain the gap between the two age groups?
In Bosnia and Herzegovina, nearly one in three economically active 15- to 24-year-olds were unemployed in the second quarter of 2026. That was the highest rate among the countries analysed. In Malta, which had the lowest rate, the figure was about one in 15. Across the EU, it was about one in six.
If we compare the two age groups, the EU youth unemployment rate was 15.6% in the same period, three times the rate for 25- to 74-year-olds (5.2%), according to Eurostat.
The rate covers only people in the labour force, meaning those who are working or actively looking for work.
That gap varies widely across Europe. In Poland, for example, youth unemployment was below the EU rate, yet it was more than four times the rate among 25- to 74-year-olds. Where is the gap widest, and what helps explain it?
Youth unemployment is highest in the Balkans
Among the 35 European countries in the data, youth unemployment is highest in Bosnia and Herzegovina at 32.2%. Romania (30.7%) and North Macedonia (29%) follow.
Countries where at least one in five young people in the labour force cannot find a job include Sweden (24.9%), Serbia (24.2%), Spain (23.9%), Finland (23.2%), Estonia (22.8%), France (21.6%) and Croatia (20%).
In these countries, many young people struggle to find a first job and gain the work experience that employers ask for.
Youth unemployment is lowest in Malta and Germany
Malta (6.8%) and Germany (7.3%) have the lowest rates. The Netherlands (8.6%), Switzerland (9.2%) and Austria (9.7%) are also below 10%.
Youth unemployment also varies widely among the EU's four largest economies. While the rate is 7.3% in Germany, it is much higher in the other three: 18.2% in Italy, 21.6% in France and 23.9% in Spain.
Where is the unemployment gap between age groups widest?
But comparing youth unemployment rates across countries does not show the full picture. Youth unemployment may be low by European standards and still be high compared with the rate in the older age group in the same country.
There are two ways to measure this gap. One is the difference between the two rates in percentage points. The other is a ratio, the youth rate divided by the rate in the older age group, which shows how many times as high the youth rate is.
Romania has the widest gap on both measures. The difference is 25.5 percentage points, and the youth rate is 5.9 times the rate in the older age group.
In Croatia and the UK, the youth rate is at least five times the rate in the older age group. Youth unemployment is 20% in Croatia and 15.6% in the UK, compared with 3.8% and 3.1%, respectively, in the older age group.
Low youth unemployment can still mask a wide gap
Some countries with fairly low youth unemployment still have a wide gap. In Poland, the youth rate is 11.8%, but the rate in the older age group is only 2.8%. In Czechia, the rates are 10.4% and 2.6%. In Norway, they are 13% and 3.1%, respectively. In all three, the youth rate is around four times the rate in the older age group.
In other countries, unemployment is relatively high in both age groups, but the relative gap is smaller. For instance, Spain has one of the highest youth unemployment rates, at 23.9%, but the rate among 25- to 74-year-olds is also high, at 9%. That puts the youth rate at 2.7 times the rate in the older age group, below the EU ratio of three. In Greece, the youth rate is 18.4%, compared with 7.7% in the older age group, giving a ratio of 2.4.
Higher youth unemployment is normal, but the gap matters
Experts say part of the gap is normal. “A combination of factors makes it ‘natural’ that the youth unemployment rate is higher than the adult unemployment rate,” Sara Elder, head of the Employment Analysis and Economic Policy Unit at the International Labour Organization (ILO), told Euronews Business.
She noted that lack of experience is a leading reason. Young people often know less about the labour market and have less experience of looking for work. Employers may choose someone with more experience instead.
Young people may also take time to "shop around" for the right job. Measurement plays a role too. Young people who stay in education longer and are neither working nor looking for work are outside the labour force. So are those who give up looking for a job. Both groups are left out when the youth unemployment rate is calculated.
When fewer young people are in work, the same number of jobseekers makes up a larger share of the youth labour force. That can help explain part of the gap between the two age groups.
Young people also tend to be the last to be hired and the first to lose their jobs in a downturn. "Youth are more vulnerable than adults in difficult economic times," Elder said.
Like young couples, young workers break up more often
"Part of the gap is natural. Young people are at the start of their careers," Professor Michael Siegenthaler, head of the Labour Market Research Division at KOF Swiss Economic Institute at ETH Zurich, told Euronews Business.
He underlined that young people move from education into work, try out different jobs and look for the right match. This search takes time.
Juan J. Dolado, honorary professor at the Carlos III University of Madrid, compared it to personal life. "Just as romantic relationships break up more frequently when people are young, the same is true for employment relationships between firms and workers," he said.
He emphasised that young people often do not fully understand their first jobs, and employers need time to see what these workers can do.
What is a normal gap?
Elder says the ratio can help identify where young jobseekers face extra barriers.
"Given the different systemic tendencies of each cohort, a ratio of the youth-to-adult unemployment rate that falls in the range of 2 to 3 could be considered a natural base. Ratios above 3, however, suggest the presence of a particular hardship (or hardships) faced by young people in their job search compared to adults," Elder said.
She noted that the extremely low ratios in Austria, Germany and Switzerland reflect how well these countries support young people as they move from school or training into work.
“This happens most visibly in their dual track education systems and subsidised apprenticeship programmes for young people following technical fields,” she said.
Siegenthaler added that unlike more school-based education systems, apprenticeships combine classroom learning with training inside a company in these countries.
Dolado pointed out that the ratio tends to be much higher in countries where the main way for youngsters to access the labour market is via short-term temporary contracts, which lead to high staff turnover.
He warned that this can have a long-term impact. Dismissals or very short contracts can leave "scarring effects" on young people's future careers, he said.

noticias.titulo: Santiago Abascal: Spain’s far-right kingmaker
noticias.resumen: The man who built Vox into Spain’s most successful far-right force now faces his biggest test: translating electoral gains into a lasting role in government.
noticias.texto: Santiago Abascal: Spain’s far-right kingmaker The man who built Vox into Spain’s most successful ultranationalist force now faces his biggest test: translating electoral gains into a lasting role in government. By AITOR HERNANDEZ-MORALES in Madrid Spanish far-right party Vox’s leader Santiago Abascal delivers a speech about culture at the Carlos de Amberes Foundation in Madrid on July 10, 2023. Thomas Coex/AFP via Getty Images Santiago Abascal has spent much of his career railing against Spain’s political establishment. Now, he is poised to join it. After Sunday’s election, the combative 50-year-old from the Basque Country is set to lead the far right into national government for the first time since the restoration of democracy in the 1970s. The polls point to a right-wing majority, with Alberto Núñez Feijóo ’s center-right People’s Party on course to finish first. But his margin of victory over Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is expected to be narrow, meaning the PP will need Abascal’s ultranationalist Vox party to form a governing majority. That gives Abascal significant power as Spain’s kingmaker although, for now, he is keeping his cards close to his chest. He has yet to spell out whether he would enter a coalition as the PP’s junior partner, what ministries he might seek or what concessions he would demand from Feijóo. His far-right agenda , however, is clear and would set the next Spanish government on a very different trajectory from Sánchez’s administration, which has prioritized multilateralism , the integration of migrants and the green economy. By contrast, Abascal wants to lock in “national priority” policies granting Spaniards preferential access to public benefits, carry out mass deportations of immigrants, roll back labor regulations and scrap climate rules. Even if he does formally join with the PP after Nov. 29, the big question is whether he will stay the course and keep the government stable. Feijóo casts himself as a moderate and sober manager , whereas Abascal is a fiery ideologue who has split from the PP in the past — both quitting the party personally, and pulling Vox out of regional coalitions with the center right. At rallies during the current campaign, the Vox leader has described the general election as “existential” for Spain, insisting that “everything is at stake” and that it is “now or never.” “This is the last opportunity for a vast majority of Spaniards, and we are not going to waste it,” he said at a rally in Madrid shortly after Sánchez called the snap election . Abascal’s leverage would have been unthinkable in 2019, when Vox first entered parliament after winning 24 of 350 seats in the hemicycle. Since then, the party has advanced its ambitions by joining the PP in numerous regional governments and taking control of dozens of municipalities. But he is now reaping the full benefit from a decade-long erosion in support for the traditional left and right, and is expected to double his haul from the 2023 election to claim about 60 seats. “Since 2023, every political party in Spain has declined — only Vox has grown,” he said at a packed rally in Alicante last week, claiming only Vox could ensure Sánchez would not pull off another political comeback, as he did three years ago. “A vote for Vox is the only thing that guarantees change,” he added, drawing a roar of approval from supporters who see little distinction between the man and his party. Abascal, who did not respond to a request for an interview for this article, is not simply Vox’s candidate or spokesman, but its undisputed driving force and the central figure of a campaign built around his persona and rhetoric. “He has a natural knack for leadership,” Vox MEP Jorge Martín Frías, who heads the party’s Disenso think tank, said in a recent interview with POLITICO. He pointed not only to Abascal’s charismatic appeal among his own supporters — a recent YouGov poll gave him a rating of 7.9 out of 10 among prospective Vox voters, ahead of Sánchez’s 7.5 among Socialists and Feijóo’s 6.9 among PP supporters — but also to the relationships he has built with far-right leaders around the world, including Argentina’s Javier Milei, Italy’s Giorgia Meloni and France’s Marine Le Pen. The Basque who went all in on Spain Born in Bilbao in 1976, Abascal hails from a region scarred by decades of separatist violence: the Basque Country. He grew up in Amurrio, a small industrial town of around 10,000 people in the province of Álava’s green, wooded Ayala valley, where his family was a fixture of local politics. His grandfather Manuel, a veteran of Francisco Franco’s forces during the civil war, was appointed mayor of Amurrio by the dictatorship in 1963. He held the post until 1979, when he was defeated by the Basque Nationalist Party in the first local elections after Spain’s transition to democracy. Abascal’s father, Santiago Abascal Escuza, was also a prominent local politician, representing the conservative Alianza Popular, the party that later became the PP. The family’s political affiliations made it a target of ETA, the Basque separatist terrorist group whose decades-long campaign of violence included the assassinations of dozens of conservative politicians. The militants attempted to extort Abascal’s grandfather, set fire to his father’s textile shop and even painted insults on the family’s horses. Abascal followed in his family’s footsteps, joining the PP in 1994. He, too, became a target. In his 2014 memoir, he recalled how a group of hooded assailants stormed the University of Deusto in Bilbao, where he was studying sociology, and daubed threats across the walls, doors and blackboards of the faculty. Days later, leaflets bearing his photograph in the crosshairs of a gun sight appeared in the corridors, warning him to “leave the Basque Country or face the consequences.” The 1997 murder of Miguel Ángel Blanco, a 29-year-old PP councilor in the nearby town of Ermua, sparked national outrage and brought the threat facing the party’s Basque activists into sharp focus. Two years later, at 23, Abascal was elected to as a councillor in Llodio, a town between Amurrio and Bilbao. The move obliged him to live under police protection for the next decade. Women hold a placard reading ‘No more lies. No more cheating truces’ with a picture of PP murdered politician ‘Miguel Angel Blanco’ after a demonstration called by AVT (Victims of Terrorism Association) at Colon Square on October 27, 2013 in Madrid, Spain. | Pablo Blazquez Dominguez/Getty Images For Guillermo Fernández Vázquez, a political scientist at Madrid’s Carlos III University who has spent years studying Vox, Abascal’s formative years in the Basque Country help explain his pugnacious style. Growing up in a small town where supporting the PP could carry serious risks, he said, instilled in him “a personal idea of resistance, of strength” — and an instinct to stand his ground at all costs. “He has these almost old-timey ideas of loyalty, courage and honor,” he said. “And these principles make him tremendously inflexible.” Abascal spent nearly two decades in the PP, serving as a councilor, provincial representative and regional lawmaker. After failing to retain his seat in the Basque Parliament in 2009, his loyalty to the party was rewarded with two well-paid appointments in institutions funded by Madrid’s regional government. Initially, he served as head of the capital region’s Data Protection Agency from 2010 until it was abolished in 2012. The following year, he was appointed director of the Foundation for Sponsorship and Social Patronage , a two-person body tasked with encouraging businesses to fund social projects. Although the foundation’s own accounts acknowledged that it failed to fulfil its core mission, Abascal was paid an annual salary of €82,492 — more than four times Spain’s then-median salary of €19,029 — plus a productivity bonus. The appointments have since fueled accusations that he made a career out of living off public cash, including through “ chiringuitos ,” a word Spaniards use to refer to both makeshift beach bars and government bodies that serve only to reward political allies. Abascal himself admits the foundation he directed was pointless — but argues that the experience gave him valuable, first-hand knowledge of useless entities which Vox now vows to eliminate. The birth of Vox Shortly after the Foundation for Sponsorship and Social Patronage was shut down as part of austerity-related cuts in Madrid in 2013, Abascal broke with the PP. At the time, he said his departure was prompted by the party’s drift toward the center under Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy, who governed Spain from 2011 to 2018. Despite promising to reverse Spain’s progressive abortion legislation and pledging not to raise taxes, Rajoy’s government did the opposite. But for Abascal, the ultimate betrayal was Rajoy’s effort to pacify the Basque Country and encourage ETA’s dissolution by improving conditions for the militant group’s prisoners and approving the release of some of its most notorious members. “The party leadership has betrayed our values and our ideas,” he wrote in an open letter announcing his resignation. Fernández Vázquez at Carlos III University argues that Abascal’s break with the PP over its approach to the Basque Country reflected something fundamental about his character: “He is, in his essence, a Spanish nationalist.” “The idea of the nation — its history, unity and place in the world — is the central thread running through his political career,” he added. Vox’s national vision of Spanish identity is likewise focal to its message. It opposes Catalan and Basque separatism , is hostile to immigration and rejects what it describes as “globalist” ideas on climate policy and “woke” social progressivism . Although outside elected politics after breaking with the PP, Abascal remained active on its fringes, tapping into growing discontent among conservatives who felt the party had become more concerned with projecting an image of responsible management than fighting on cultural and national questions. Santiago Abascal, leader of Spain’s far-right party VOX, gives a speech during a campaign meeting ahead of regional elections in Andalusia, on November 26, 2018 in Granada. | Cristina Quicler/AFP via Getty Images In 2014, he returned to public life with Vox , a party he presented as the authentic defender of the PP’s classic ideas and values. In the years since, Fernández Vázquez said, Vox has invested heavily in building an ideological project, “seeking not only to win over disaffected conservative voters, but to eventually even pull Abascal’s former party over to adopt their positions.” Vox’s messaging has also shifted over time. Pablo Simón, a political scientist at Madrid’s Carlos III University, said that while the party initially focused on Spanish nationalism and opposition to regional separatism, it had more recently placed immigration at the center of its strategy and coordinated closely with allies in the European Patriots group. The result, Fernández Vázquez said, is a party that has increasingly become “ a communications node, a bridge, a hinge between the new Latin American right, the European far right and the Trumpist right ” — and whose domestic agenda increasingly echoes theirs. “Enough of having to put up with anyone who enters Spain being allowed to stay in Spain forever!” Abascal told supporters in Alicante earlier this week. Mirroring U.S. President Donald Trump in his vow to take all measures — even those currently prohibited by law — to stop the flow of migrants into the country, Vox’s leader promised: “We are standing in the election to make legal what they tell us is illegal today.” The kingmaker Abascal cultivates an image of a man more at home in Spain’s forested mountains than in the corridors of power in Madrid. The far-right leader is an avid birdwatcher , a passion he developed as a youngster, when he would spend weekends roaming the densely wooded hills around Amurrio. While most Spanish politicians are football obsessives, Abascal is curiously indifferent to the sport — so much so that in May 2026 he came close to alienating a sizeable chunk of Seville’s football-mad public by casually pulling on a Sevilla FC shirt , apparently oblivious to its fierce rivalry with the city’s other team, Real Betis. Leader of the Spanish far-right party Vox, Santiago Abascal gives a press conference in Madrid, on November 13, 2019. | Gabriel Bouys/AFP via Getty Images But he has other more conventionally macho pursuits. His passion for motorcycles is evident on his social media pages, and despite his love of birds, he has a growing interest in hunting , a long-standing pastime of Spain’s well-heeled conservative set. For all the bravura of his incendiary speeches, Abascal is a politically introverted figure who surrounds himself with a small circle of trusted advisers — a cadre that has changed dramatically in recent years. Many of Vox’s early leading figures have left or been pushed aside , consolidating the influence of key lieutenants such as Kiko Méndez-Monasterio , often described as the party’s eminence grise , secretary-general Ignacio Garriga and MEPs Jorge Buxadé and Jorge Martin Frías . That makes it all the more likely that the future direction of Spanish politics will be shaped by Abascal himself. If the PP needs Vox to govern after Sunday’s election, Abascal could secure a place in the Cabinet — potentially even the deputy premiership — and a substantial say over policy. But some in Madrid believe he has noted how Matteo Salvini, leader of Italy’s far-right Lega Party, has lost political prominence as a junior partner in Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s governing coalition. In a bid to avoid the same fate, Vox could stay outside government, allowing the PP to govern as a minority administration with the far right’s support in parliament — and leaving Abascal free to distance his party from any unpopular decisions. Simón considers that scenario possible, but unlikely. “It would be surprising if they don’t join the government,” he said, arguing it would be difficult for the party not to succumb to the temptation of running ministries and exercising direct power. Depending on how many seats it wins on Sunday, he added, the party would be in a position to demand a sizeable share of the spoils and exert considerable power within the cabinet. Vox’s MEP Martín Frías characterizes Abascal as a leader who is comfortable building relationships across ideological and national boundaries, working with “a common diagnosis” even when there isn’t “a common program.” But Fernández Vázquez said the pragmatism Abascal has shown when teaming up with right-wing heavyweights such as Meloni and Milei on the international stage may be harder to replicate in Madrid, where he has lingering personal grievances. “There’s still deep resentment toward the PP, a party he considered his own, one that he believes betrayed fundamental values and abandoned him and other like-minded figures,” he said. That tension could emerge in any dealings with Feijóo, who last week pitched himself to voters by declaring , “I know what governing means; I have governed. I know what managing means; I have managed, and that is what Spain needs.” For Abascal, it is precisely this kind of managerial politics — focused on competence and stability rather than ideological combat — that helped drive him out of the PP. The far-right leader could also clash with Borja Sémper, the PP’s campaign spokesman, who also hails from the Basque Country, but from the bustling city of Irun. A moderate who defends Spain’s existing abortion law, supports LGBTQ+ rights and has expressed openness to the regularization of undocumented migrants, he embodies much of what Abascal dislikes in his former party. Tense teamwork There are precedents for what could soon be Spain’s national government. In 2022, the PP and Vox entered into their first regional coalition in Castilla y León, where relations were strained by Vox’s attempts to push an anti-abortion protocol and replace legislation on gender-based violence with its preferred concept of “intrafamily violence.” But in Valencia, where a coalition was forged the following year, the relationship functioned relatively smoothly , with the two parties passing budgets and advancing a shared legislative agenda. Both experiments, along with similar coalitions in Extremadura, Aragón and Murcia, came to an abrupt end in July 2024, when Vox withdrew from its five regional governments with the PP after the latter agreed to meet its legal obligation to relocate unaccompanied migrant minors from the Canary Islands to mainland Spain. The walkouts left the PP governing in minority administrations, dependent on Vox’s goodwill to pass legislation in the regional parliaments. Fernández Vázquez predicted a national coalition could face the same fate if Feijóo tries to limit Vox’s influence or treat Abascal as a junior partner. “Do I think Vox will enter into a coalition government? Yes,” he said. “Will it remain in that government until the legislative term ends? No.” While Abascal may relish describing the election as “existential” for Spain — it’s probably also the case for his party, which may not get another chance to enter national government. “There are opportunities that come along only once in a lifetime,” he said in Alicante this week. “We have hope because we have faith in God, in our families, in our homeland Spain and in this movement that is Vox.”

noticias.titulo: Ein Spaziergang mit Markus Frohnmaier
noticias.resumen: Präsentiert von YouTube.
noticias.texto: Listen on Spotify Apple Music Amazon Music Ein Ende der Ukraine-Hilfen, Verständnis für russische Einflusssphären und enge Drähte zur amerikanischen MAGA-Bewegung: Die außenpolitischen Visionen der AfD brechen radikal mit dem bisherigen Kurs der Union, der SPD und der Grünen. Markus Frohnmaier, enger Vertrauter von Alice Weidel und außenpolitischer Sprecher der Partei, skizziert beim Spaziergang mit Gordon Repinski durch das Berliner Regierungsviertel eine neue geopolitische Ausrichtung. Warum fordert der AfD-Politiker ein Ende der Sanktionen gegen Russland und lehnt Sicherheitsgarantien für die Ukraine strikt ab? Im Gespräch offenbart sich nicht nur der Blick der Partei auf den Ukraine-Krieg und den Anschlag auf die Nord-Stream-Pipelines, sondern auch eine Verteidigung des umstrittenen Konzepts der „Remigration“. Repinski hakt nach, wie die AfD ihre Machtansprüche mit Alice Weidel als Kanzlerkandidatin und Tino Chrupalla an der Spitze realisieren will und warum die deutsche Erinnerungskultur umgebaut werden soll. Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig. noticias.titulo: [Interview] Putin’s latest wonder weapon – a nuclear-armed ‘Death Star’ satellite – may be ‘sheer hysteria’, expert warns
noticias.resumen: There is no open-source evidence that Russia is about to launch a nuclear-armed satellite over the EU's head, in what sounded like Western paranoia about Vladimir Putin's supposed "wonder-weapons".
noticias.texto: There is no open-source evidence that Russia is about to launch a nuclear-armed satellite over the EU’s head, in what sounds like more hype and speculation about Moscow’s “wonder-weapons”. According to German media reports earlier this week (24 November), the nuclear-capable “Sputnik-S” has been built, is being stored in Moscow, and was to be launched in the next 60 days. Those reports cited German and wider Western intelligence sources. US intelligence had already warned allies about the project in 2024, The New York Times reported then . If the Sputnik-S was designed to nuke Western satellite systems, it could destroy even the Starlink clusters vital to the US military, but related debris would also destroy Russian and Chinese satellites, making it a weapon of last resort. If it detonated nuclear bombs at high-altitude, between 300km and 400km above the earth, as the US and Russia did in Cold War-era tests in the 1960s, Sputnik-S could also cause an electromagnetic pulse that blew out streetlights, phone lines, and started fires at power stations, but without directly killing people, the old tests showed. And if it was being stored in Moscow, it was probably in the Reutovo district, where NPO Mashinostroyeniya, its likely manufacturer, was based, according to Bart Hendrickx, a Belgian writer on space affairs, who contributes to The Space Review magazine . It would likely be launched from the military Plesetsk cosmodrome, near Arkhangelsk, in northwestern Russia, probably into a circular orbit 2,000km above the earth, with an inclination of 67 degrees, after its rocket had detached its first and second stages above Russian territory, then its third and fourth ones over the Pacific Ocean, Hendrickx said. Read more Russian satellite manoeuvring toward EU spying-risk zone Satellites were usually shipped from Moscow to Plesetsk “several weeks” before take-off, to be mated with launch vehicles. But Western spy satellites would see the rocket being rolled out to its launch pad only 48 hours before take-off, Hendrickx added, which meant German intelligence must have had a human source in Russia, who told them about a 60-day plan. noticias.titulo: Czech Republic used to be one of the EU’s most fiscally conservative hawks, now it demands more cash
noticias.resumen: Through his ultimatums for a higher EU budget, Czech prime minister Andrej Babiš has manufactured ammunition for his anti-EU political allies across the continent. Europe will remember Czech Republic for its self-centred, arrogant and cunning approach to EU long-term budget negotiations
noticias.texto: First published in Respekt. When the Czech Republic joined the EU, a story was told about the country’s membership of this prestigious member’s club. 22 years ago, Czechs told themselves that bloc accession was merely a return of a great European nation to a group it had always belonged to. Czech Europeanism was controlled by the centre-right. Under the Czech doctrine, informed by liberal economics theory, the EU was to become more pragmatic, rational and efficient. Like the Anglo-Saxons, the Czechs thought they would debate wasteful agricultural policy, bloated subsidies and shortcomings in European competitiveness. Brexit complicated our political orientation towards the UK, a bastion of political rationality. It was no longer clear who in the EU should serve as the Czech Republic’s model ally on key economic and constitutional questions. Czech political parties dared not point to their neighbours: Germany, a dominant economic power; or Poland, deemed too behind. Public debate gave the impression that Czechs saw themselves as almost on Scandinavia, where people did not believe in the euro and everything worked as it should. Then a man named Andrej Babiš rose to prominence; he was elected prime minister twice.
